covers.quote: Use 70 characters or fewer

rules.quote: Write headings that are no more than 70 characters (including spaces).
rules.violation_condition: a heading containing more than 70 characters including spaces
rules.why: Specific rule with exact character count limit (G-4).

covers.quote: Starting a heading with ‘why’, ‘how’ or ‘what’ makes it slower for the user to read.

rules.violation_condition: a heading phrased as a question (ending with a question mark or starting with question words like 'why', 'how', 'what')
rules.why: Clear structural instruction against interrogative headings.

covers.quote: Use keywords to start headings
Using keywords at the start of a heading is called ‘frontloading’.

examples.note: Example under 'Write this' showing frontloaded keywords.

parts.quote: Write a heading starting with the main keywords

rules.quote: Start headings and subheadings with keywords that help people to make a connection.
rules.specification: Frontload headings by placing key nouns/topics in the first 2-3 words rather than lead-in verbs or generic descriptors.
rules.violation_condition: a heading or subheading that does not frontload key information or begins with filler/empty words
rules.why: Consolidated frontloading rule with its direct examples (G-4, E-2).

covers.quote: State the main point

rules.quote: Don’t use empty words or phrases (for example, ‘more’ or ‘related information’).
rules.violation_condition: a heading using empty words or phrases such as 'more' or 'related information'
rules.why: Clear prohibition against uninformative/empty heading phrases (E-2).

covers.quote: Write headings in a complete organised hierarchy.

examples.note: Logical hierarchical structure without skipped levels.

parts.quote: H1: Apply for a drivers licence

examples.note: Skipping directly from H1 to H3.

rules.violation_condition: a heading whose level increases by more than 1 relative to the immediately preceding heading (e.g. H1 followed directly by H3)
rules.why: Standard heading hierarchy rule with explicit compliant and violating examples (E-2, E-3).

covers.quote: Use one level 1 heading
In documents, use level 1 headings (or ‘Heading 1’ style) for the main sections, such as part titles.

rules.quote: Use just one level 1 heading per webpage.
rules.violation_condition: a webpage having zero or more than one level 1 heading (H1)
when: Applies to webpages; printed documents may use level 1 headings for main sections/part titles.
rules.why: Specific quantitative rule for H1 on webpages, noting document exception (G-2, G-4).

covers.quote: Avoid level 5 and deeper heading levels
You can use deeper heading levels (level 4 and below) for very complex documents, but try to avoid it.

rules.quote: Try to use only 3 or 4 heading levels at the most.
rules.violation_condition: using level 5 or deeper headings (H5, H6, etc.)
when: Can be relaxed for very complex documents.
rules.why: Clear structural limit on heading depth (G-2, G-3).

covers.quote: Space out headings

rules.quote: Separate each heading from the next one by some text, even if it’s only a sentence.
rules.violation_condition: two headings appearing immediately adjacent with no body text between them
rules.why: Clear structural requirement forbidding back-to-back headings without text (G-4).

covers.quote: Create at least 2 headings for each level

rules.quote: Give each heading level in a section at least one other heading at the same level.
rules.violation_condition: a single isolated heading of a given level under its parent section (a stranded subheading)
rules.why: Clear structural rule requiring at least two siblings per heading level in a section (G-4).

covers.quote: Use numbered headings only for steps
If you use numbered headings, use them only in the body.
Don’t use numbered headings in the preliminary pages or endmatter in a report.
Don’t number more than the first 3 heading levels.

rules.quote: Use numbered headings only when they relate to a series of steps.
rules.specification: Flag headings beginning with numbers (e.g. '1.', '2.1') unless in an explicit stepwise procedure or permitted print cross-referencing.
rules.violation_condition: a heading containing numbering when it does not describe a sequential step or process, or numbered headings in preliminary pages/endmatter or past level 3 in print
when: In print, numbered headings can be used for cross-referencing in the body.
In print, do not use numbered headings in preliminary pages or endmatter.
In print, do not number more than the first 3 heading levels.
rules.why: Single rule governing when numbered headings are permitted, absorbing print qualifications (G-2).

covers.quote: Be consistent: use a parallel structure
All headings in a level should be consistent.

rules.violation_condition: headings at the same hierarchical level within a section using inconsistent grammatical forms (e.g. mixing imperative instructions with noun phrases)
rules.why: Parallelism rule for headings of the same level (G-4).

covers.quote: Don’t add an underline

rules.quote: Don’t underline headings or any other text.
rules.violation_condition: text that is underlined (using HTML <u>, style text-decoration: underline, or markdown underline formatting)
rules.why: Direct formatting prohibition against underlines (G-4).

covers.quote: Apply HTML elements, tags and styles to headings
Use the correct HTML element for the heading level.
Apply correct inbuilt heading styles so they can be automatically added to navigation and contents pages.

rules.quote: Use styles, tags and HTML elements to identify headings in digital content.
rules.violation_condition: a heading represented solely by visual styling (like bold or font size) rather than structural heading elements or tags (h1-h6)
rules.why: Consolidates semantic markup/tagging rules for digital headings (G-1, G-4).

covers.quote: Write all headings in sentence case and use minimal punctuation
Don’t write headings in all capital letters as users could misread words.

rules.quote: Use sentence case for headings to help people read the text more easily.
rules.violation_condition: a heading written in title case or all capital letters
when: Capitalise proper nouns, acronyms, and initialisms.
rules.why: Standard capitalisation rule for headings, consolidating prohibition on all-caps (G-2, G-4).

covers.quote: Even if the heading is a sentence, it doesn’t need a full stop at the end.

rules.quote: Don’t use a full stop to end headings
rules.violation_condition: a heading ending with a full stop
when: Even if the heading is a complete sentence.
rules.why: Punctuation rule specifically banning full stops at the end of headings (G-4).

covers.quote: Avoid using shortened forms in headings

rules.quote: Don’t use a shortened form in a heading unless it is better known than the full term (for example, ‘DNA’ and ‘CSIRO’).
rules.specification: Check shortened forms against a whitelist of universally known acronyms (e.g. DNA, CSIRO, ABC); flag others.
rules.violation_condition: an abbreviation, acronym, or initialism in a heading that is not widely recognized/better known than its spelled-out form
when: Exception for terms that are better known than the full term.
rules.why: Rule restricting shortened forms in headings, with known-form exception (G-2, G-4).
